A2.text:
Aysel's older sister, Gunel, is a photographer. Her camera is very expensive. Last month, Aysel went to Gabala with her friend Lala, and she asked to borrow the camera.

“Be very careful with it,” Gunel said.

In Gabala, Aysel was careless. She put the camera on a bench and took a selfie with her phone. Then she turned around, and the camera fell on the stones. The lens was broken.

At home, Gunel saw the camera. “What happened?” she asked.

Aysel was scared. “Lala dropped it,” she said. “It was not my fault.” She wanted to blame her friend.

Gunel called Lala. Lala was surprised and hurt. “I did not even touch it!” she said.

That night, Aysel could not sleep. She felt a lot of regret. In the morning, she went to her sister's room.

“I lied,” Aysel said. “I broke the camera. I did not do it on purpose, but I want to apologise. I'm sorry.”

Gunel was quiet. Then she said, “There's no use crying over spilled milk. But next time, bite your tongue before you blame your friend.”

Aysel worked in a café for two months to make up for her mistake. She paid for a new lens. She also said sorry to Lala.

Gunel and Lala decided to forgive her. Aysel learned an important lesson. Sometimes you learn the hard way.

B1.text:
Gunel was a wedding photographer, and her camera was the most valuable thing she owned. So when her younger sister Aysel asked to borrow it for a weekend in Gabala with her friend Lala, Gunel hesitated for a long time. “Fine,” she said at last. “But it never leaves your neck.”

It left Aysel's neck on the second afternoon. They had stopped at a viewpoint above the lake, and Aysel, wanting a selfie with the mountains, put the camera down on a low stone wall. It was a careless moment, nothing more. When she turned back, her elbow knocked it, and it fell onto the rocks below. The lens cracked from one side to the other.

She didn't tell Gunel until she got home, and when her sister saw the damage, panic took over. “Lala dropped it,” Aysel heard herself say. “I told her to be careful.”

Gunel phoned Lala that evening. Lala listened in shocked silence and then said quietly, “I never even held it.” She hung up, and she didn't answer Aysel's messages.

For two nights, Aysel lay awake. The regret was worse than any punishment. She had broken a camera by accident, but she had chosen to blame her friend on purpose.

On the third morning, she knocked on her sister's door. “I lied,” she said. “It was me. I want to apologise — to you and to Lala.”

Gunel looked at her for a long moment. “There's no use crying over spilled milk,” she said finally. “Cameras can be fixed. But next time, bite your tongue before you put your mistake on someone else.”

Aysel took a job at a café on Nizami Street and worked every weekend for two months to make up for what she had done. She paid for the new lens herself and wrote Lala a long letter.

It took Lala a while to forgive her. Aysel didn't blame her for that. Some lessons, she decided, you can only learn the hard way.

B2.text:
Gunel's camera was less a possession than a member of the family. It had paid for her first car, photographed two hundred weddings and survived a fall into the Kura river; she spoke of it with the tenderness most people reserve for pets. So when her younger sister Aysel asked to borrow it for a weekend in Gabala with her friend Lala, Gunel took a full day to answer. “One condition,” she said. “It never leaves your neck.”

It left Aysel's neck on the second afternoon. At a viewpoint above the Nohur lake, wanting a selfie with the mountains behind her, she rested the camera on a low stone wall — a careless gesture lasting perhaps ten seconds. Turning back, she caught it with her elbow and watched it tumble onto the rocks. The lens was split from rim to rim.

She said nothing for the rest of the trip. At home, confronted by her sister's horrified face, she felt panic close around her throat, and a sentence came out before she had decided to say it: “Lala dropped it. I warned her.”

Gunel rang Lala that evening. There was a long pause on the line. “I never even touched it,” Lala said evenly, and hung up. After that, Aysel's messages went unanswered.

Aysel lay awake for two nights, and the regret was worse than any punishment Gunel could have invented. The accident she could live with. What she couldn't forgive herself for was the choice — the decision, made in a second of fear, to blame someone who trusted her, entirely on purpose.

On the third morning she stood in her sister's doorway. “I lied,” she said. “It was me, and I let Lala take the blame. I need to apologise to both of you.”

Gunel studied her for a long time. “No use crying over spilled milk,” she said eventually. “Lenses can be replaced. Friends are harder. Next time, bite your tongue before you hand your mistake to somebody else.”

Aysel found weekend work at a café on Nizami Street and spent two months carrying trays to make up for it. She paid for the new lens to the last manat and wrote Lala a letter she rewrote six times.

Forgiveness, when it came, came slowly — and Aysel didn't resent the wait. Some lessons, she understood now, you only learn the hard way.

podcast.title: The wrong Tony

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Have you ever sent a message to the wrong person? Guess: who got Sam's message about the boring meeting?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is mistakes and regrets. And I made a big one on Monday.
[laugh] Oh no. What did you do?
I wrote a message to my friend about my boss: "The meeting was so boring, he talked for two hours." And I sent it… to my boss.
No! How?
Careless. My friend is Tom, my boss is Tony. Their names are next to each other on my phone.
What happened next?
I went to his office and apologised. I said it wasn't on purpose, and that the meeting wasn't really boring.
Was it boring?
[laugh] Very. But he was kind. He said, "You're right, Sam. Next time I'll make it shorter."
Wow, a good boss. So you can't blame yourself too much.
I'm trying. But now I check every message three times. Sometimes you learn the hard way.
My biggest regret is something I said to my sister when I was nineteen. We had a silly argument about clothes, and I said something really unkind.
Did you make friends again quickly?
Not for two months. I was too proud to say sorry. My grandmother told me, "Sometimes it's better to bite your tongue."
Wise woman. How did it end?
I bought her favourite cake and wrote her a long letter. I wanted to make up for those two months.
And did she forgive you?
She did. She said, "I forgive you — but the cake is mine."
[chuckle] That's sisters. I think "sorry" is the hardest word — and the most important one.
I agree. Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: tell your partner about a mistake you made — and what you learned from it.
And check who you're sending it to. See you next time!
Bye for now!
